procedural_history.originating_court: District Magistrate of Purulia (for Guhiram Gope) and District Magistrate, Midnapore (for Subodh Chandra Barik)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of detention passed against the petitioners under s. 3(1)(a)(ii) and (iii) read with s. 3(2) of the Preventive Detention Act, IV of 1950.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The petitioner (Barik) filed a petition in the High Court at Calcutta against the said order but that was dismissed.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Petition under Art. 32 of the Constitution of India for the enforcement of fundamental rights. The petition came up for hearing on April 11. 1969 before Sikri and Bachawat, JJ. who referred it to a larger Bench as the question involved in this petition was of substantial importance.

directions: Petitioners 15 and 36 to be set at liberty forthwith.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appropriate Government has an obligation to consider the representation made by a detenue.

facts: Petitioners were detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950.
They made representations to the State Government against their detention after their cases had been referred to an Advisory Board.
The State Government did not consider the representations itself but instead passed them on to the Advisory Board for consideration.
law: The key legal provision is Article 22(5) of the Constitution, which guarantees a detenue the right to be given the earliest opportunity to make a representation against their detention order.
application: The Court reasoned that the constitutional right to make a representation, guaranteed by Article 22(5), necessarily implies a corresponding constitutional obligation on the part of the detaining authority (the Government) to consider that representation.
The purpose of this right is to allow the detenue to show that their detention is unwarranted and to give the government an opportunity to correct any errors.
The Court established that there is a "dual obligation" on the Government and a "dual right" for the detenue:
1. The detenue has the right to have their representation considered by the appropriate Government.
2. The detenue also has the right to have that same representation considered by the Advisory Board.

These two considerations are distinct. The Government considers the representation to determine if its own order is lawful and justified, while the Board considers it to form an opinion on whether there is sufficient cause for detention.

The Court rejected the argument that only the Advisory Board needs to consider the representation. It noted that for detentions of less than three months (which do not require a Board), this would render the right to representation meaningless or "nugatory."
The structure of the Preventive Detention Act also supported this view, as it requires representations to be addressed to the Government, implying it is the body intended to consider them.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appropriate Government has a constitutional obligation to consider the representation made by a detenue. This duty is separate and distinct from the obligation to forward the representation to the Advisory Board. The government's failure to consider the representation itself was a violation of the detenue's rights under Article 22(5).

issue.issue_text: Whether it makes any difference to the Government's obligation to consider a representation if it is made after the detenue's case is referred to the Advisory Board.

facts: Petitioners were detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950.
They made representations to the State Government against their detention.
Crucially, these representations were made *after* their cases had already been referred to the Advisory Board.
The State Government did not consider the representations itself; instead, it forwarded them directly to the Advisory Board for its consideration.
law: Article 22(5) of the Constitution guarantees a detenue the right to be afforded the earliest opportunity to make a representation against their detention.
The Supreme Court interpreted this to mean there is a "dual obligation" on the government and a "dual right" for the detenue.
First, the detenue has the right to have their representation considered by the appropriate Government.
Second, the detenue has the right to have that same representation considered again by the Advisory Board.
These two considerations are distinct: the Government considers if the order is lawful and proper, while the Board considers if there is sufficient cause for detention.
application: The Court rejected the government's argument that its obligation to consider the representation ceases once the case is referred to the Advisory Board.
It reasoned that the constitutional obligation under Article 22(5) is absolute and does not make any distinction based on when the representation is made.
The Court stated that the Government's role is not merely that of a "transmitting authority" to pass documents to the Board.
The fact that the representation is addressed to the Government implies that the Government itself must apply its mind to it.
Therefore, the Government's failure to independently consider the representation, even though it was made after the referral to the Board, was a breach of its constitutional duty.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the timing of the representation does not affect the Government's constitutional obligation. The Government must independently consider a detenue's representation, even if it is submitted after the case has been referred to the Advisory Board. Simply forwarding it to the Board without its own consideration is a failure to fulfill the duty mandated by Article 22(5).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appropriate Government has an obligation to consider the representation made by a detenue.
appellant_arguments: The petitioners had a constitutional right under Article 22(5) to have their representation considered by the State Government.
The constitutional right to make a representation includes, by necessary implication, the right to a consideration of that representation by the detaining authority to whom it is made.
The government cannot simply act as a transmitting authority to pass the representation to the Advisory Board without considering it first.
The power of the government under Section 13 to revoke or modify a detention order implies that it must consider the representation to decide if such action is warranted.
respondent_arguments: Neither Article 22, clauses 4 and 5, nor the Preventive Detention Act, make it mandatory (either expressly or by necessary implication) for the State Government to consider the representations.
It is sufficient for the Government to pass the representations on to the Advisory Board for its consideration.

The previous court decision in Sk. Abdul Karim & Ors. v. State of West Bengal, which held that there is a legal obligation on the government to consider the representation, was not warranted by the provisions of Article 22 or the Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether it makes any difference to the Government's obligation to consider a representation if it is made after the detenue's case is referred to the Advisory Board.
appellant_arguments: The State Government has a constitutional obligation to consider the detenue's representation irrespective of whether it was made before or after the case was referred to the Advisory Board.
respondent_arguments: The obligation for the government to consider a representation is only applicable if the representation is made *before* the detenue's case is referred to the Advisory Board.
Since the petitioners made their representations after their cases were referred, the government was not obligated to consider them.
There is no practical utility in the Government considering the representations when their cases, including the representations, were already being considered by the Board.

cases.case_name: Sk. Abdul Karim v. State of West Bengal
cases.principle: A person detained under the Act has a right to make a representation, and there is a constitutional obligation on the part of the appropriate Government to consider it. The establishment of an advisory board does not relieve the Government of this separate obligation.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The constitutional right to make a representation guaranteed by Article 22(5) includes, by necessary implication, the constitutional right to have that representation considered by the detaining authority. This obligation on the detaining authority to consider the representation exists irrespective of whether it was made before or after the case was referred to the Advisory Board.
obiter: The government's consideration of the representation is to ascertain whether the detention order is in conformity with its power under the relevant law, which is a distinct function from the Advisory Board's consideration of whether there is sufficient cause for detention.
The power of the government to revoke or modify a detention order under Section 13 of the Act implies that it must consider the detenue's representation to determine if such action is warranted.
The Constitution recognizes the necessity of preventive detention on extraordinary occasions, but it also provides strict safeguards to protect personal liberty.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that Article 22(5) of the Constitution, by necessary implication, imposes a constitutional obligation on the appropriate Government to consider a detenue's representation. This duty is independent of the Advisory Board's role and is not fulfilled by merely transmitting the representation to the Board. The phrases "as soon as may be" and "the earliest opportunity" in Article 22(5) indicate that the representation is meant for the detaining authority to assess if the detention is unwarranted. This obligation on the Government to consider the representation exists irrespective of whether it is made before or after the case is referred to the Advisory Board. The State Government's failure to perform this duty violates the detenue's constitutional right and renders the detention order unsustainable.
legal_tests_applied: Implied Constitutional Obligation Test: The court determined that the constitutional right to make a representation under Article 22(5) includes, by necessary implication, the corresponding constitutional obligation for the detaining authority to consider that representation, as no other authority is specified to do so.

Statutory Purpose Test: The court analyzed Sections 7 and 13 of the Preventive Detention Act to conclude that Parliament's intent was for the Government to actively consider representations. The requirement for the representation to be addressed to the Government (s. 7) and the Government's power to revoke or modify the detention order (s. 13) would be illogical if the Government had no duty to consider the representation itself.
policy_considerations: The constitutional safeguards in Article 22 reflect the Constitution's "extreme anxiety" to protect personal liberty under Article 21 and ensure that no person is detained contrary to the law or in breach of prescribed restrictions.

The purpose of granting a detenue the "earliest opportunity" to make a representation is to enable them to demonstrate that their detention is wrongful or illegal, a purpose that can only be served if the authority that detained them considers their protest.

The Government's obligation to consider a representation is distinct from the Advisory Board's obligation. The Government considers whether the order conforms with its power under the law, while the Board opines on whether there is sufficient cause for detention. These are two separate safeguards for the detenue.
